pages.text: Two years ago, a serious knee injury brought Faris's playing career to an abrupt end before it had really begun. For weeks he refused to watch a single match, convinced that football had nothing left to offer him. It was his old coach, Mr Hamdan, who suggested he train as a junior referee instead. "You understand the game better than most players I've coached," he said. "Now learn to see it from the middle." Reluctantly, Faris agreed, and to his surprise, he discovered he had a gift for it.

By the age of sixteen, Faris had earned a reputation in Dammam's youth league for being calm, fair and almost impossible to fool. So when an email arrived appointing him to referee the regional under-18 final, he should have been delighted. Instead, his heart sank as he read the team names. One of the finalists was Al-Noor Academy, and their captain was his older brother, Saud. He read the message three times, hoping he had misunderstood.

At dinner that evening, his uncle burst out laughing when he heard the news. "Well, Saud, it looks like the trophy is already yours!" he joked. Saud grinned and nudged his brother. "You'll look after me, won't you, little referee?" Everyone laughed, but Faris barely touched his food, the words echoing uncomfortably in his head.

The next day, he told Mr Hamdan he was thinking of withdrawing from the match. The coach listened patiently, then shook his head. "The league chose you because they trust you, and the league knows who your brother is," he said. "A good referee doesn't wonder who will be angry. He asks only one question: what actually happened?" Faris left the meeting feeling slightly braver, though no less nervous.

On the night of the final, the stadium was packed and the air was thick with noise and humidity. From the first whistle, both teams played with intensity, and Faris had to keep a cool head as tempers began to flare. In the twentieth minute, he showed a yellow card to an Al-Noor defender for a reckless tackle, and he heard a few fans whistling at him. Al-Noor took the lead just before half-time, but their opponents, Al-Waha, equalised soon after the break. As the clock ticked on, the tension became almost unbearable.

In the eighty-eighth minute, Al-Waha won a corner, and every player crowded into the penalty area. The ball was whipped in, a striker headed it towards the empty net, and Saud, standing on the goal line, threw himself across to stop it. The crowd roared as the ball bounced away, and most people assumed he had blocked it with his shoulder. But Faris had a perfect view, and he knew without any doubt that the ball had struck his brother's outstretched arm.

For a split second, time seemed to freeze, and Faris felt every eye in the stadium on him. He thought of his uncle's joke, of family dinners, of how easy it would be to simply wave play on. Then he heard Mr Hamdan's voice: what actually happened? Faris blew his whistle firmly, pointed to the penalty spot and, with a trembling hand, held up a red card to his own brother. Saud stared at him in disbelief, opened his mouth to protest, and then walked off without a word.

Al-Waha's captain stepped up and calmly scored the penalty, sending their supporters into wild celebration. The final few minutes felt like hours, with angry chants from the Al-Noor fans ringing in Faris's ears. When he finally blew the full-time whistle, Al-Waha had won 2-1. Several Al-Noor players refused to shake his hand, and Faris walked towards the tunnel with his eyes fixed on the ground.

Afterwards, Faris lingered in the changing room far longer than necessary, dreading the journey home. When he eventually stepped out into the car park, he found Saud leaning against their father's car, still in his kit. Faris braced himself for an argument, but his brother simply held out a bottle of water. "It was my arm," Saud admitted quietly. "I didn't even think; it just happened in the heat of the moment."

"I'm sorry," Faris began, but Saud shook his head. "Don't apologise for doing your job properly. If you'd let it go, I'd never have been able to respect a single decision you made again." Their father, who had been watching from the driver's seat, rolled down the window and smiled. "Tonight I'm proud of both my sons," he said, "the one who accepted the truth and the one who had the courage to tell it." As they drove home, Faris realised he had lost nothing that mattered, and gained something far more valuable than a trophy.

pages.text: For eleven years, Salem and Hamza had shared everything: a desk, a bicycle with a stubborn chain, and a secret knock. It was three quick taps, a pause, then two slow ones, and it meant "It's me, open up." So when Hamza began ignoring his messages in the autumn of their final year at school, Salem took it personally. At first he made excuses for him. Perhaps his phone was broken, or he was buried under revision. But when Hamza walked straight past him in the school corridor, eyes fixed on the floor, Salem felt something inside him go cold.

The real blow came on the day of the regional science fair. They had spent months building a water filter from charcoal, sand and recycled bottles, and Hamza had promised to bring the final model. Salem waited at the entrance until the judges had started their rounds, rehearsing their presentation under his breath. Hamza never showed up. Salem was forced to explain a project he couldn't demonstrate, his cheeks burning as the judges exchanged polite, disappointed glances. "Some friend you turned out to be," he muttered as he packed up the empty table.

For the next two weeks, Salem gave Hamza the cold shoulder. He sat with other boys at lunch, laughed a little too loudly at their jokes, and pretended not to notice when Hamza glanced over. His mother, who noticed everything, asked one evening why Hamza hadn't visited lately. "Ask him yourself," Salem snapped, and he immediately regretted his tone. His mother simply raised an eyebrow and said, "Anger is a poor reader, habibi. It only reads the first page of the story."

Her words stayed with him longer than he would have liked. A few days later, Salem's uncle mentioned that Abu Hamza had been in hospital for over a month after a serious back operation. Salem stared at him, his fork frozen halfway to his mouth. Nobody at school had said a word, and Hamza certainly hadn't. "Who's running the bakery, then?" Salem asked slowly, although he had a sinking feeling that he already knew the answer.

That night he set his alarm for half past three. The streets were silent and strangely blue as he cycled through the neighbourhood, past shuttered shops and sleeping cats. Long before he reached the bakery, he could smell it: warm dough, sesame, the faint sweetness of dates. A single light was burning inside, and through the steamy window he saw Hamza alone, kneading dough with the slow rhythm of someone who hadn't slept properly in weeks. Salem raised his hand and knocked: three quick taps, a pause, then two slow ones.

Hamza froze, then opened the door, flour up to his elbows. "What are you doing here?" he asked, but there was no anger in his voice, only surprise. Salem didn't bother with a speech. He rolled up his sleeves and asked, "Where do you want me?" For a moment Hamza looked as if he might argue. Then his shoulders dropped, and he pointed to a mountain of dough waiting to be shaped.

They worked side by side until the first customers arrived at six, and somewhere between the third and fourth tray, Hamza finally explained. His father had insisted on keeping the bakery open so that the family wouldn't fall behind on the rent, and Hamza had been doing the early shift before school every single day. On the morning of the science fair, the oven had broken down, and he had spent hours waiting for a repairman. "I should have told you," he admitted, staring at his hands. "I just thought that if I said it out loud, I'd fall apart."

"You don't have to carry everything on your own," Salem replied. "That's rather the whole point of having friends." Over the following weeks, he turned up at the bakery every morning, and before long, two other boys from their class had joined the early shift as well. They took turns, revised chemistry formulas between batches of bread, and even rebuilt their water filter on the bakery's back counter. Customers began to joke that the bread had never tasted better, and nobody could quite explain why.

By the time Abu Hamza came home, walking carefully with a stick, the bakery was running like clockwork. He stood in the doorway for a long moment, watching four sleepy teenagers argue cheerfully about the right amount of salt. Later, the science teacher allowed the boys to present their filter at the end-of-year exhibition, and this time it worked perfectly. But for Salem, the real prize was something simpler: every morning before school, he heard a familiar knock on his own front door, three quick taps, a pause, then two slow ones.

pages.text: For as long as Noura could remember, a black stone had sat on the top shelf of her grandfather's majlis, between a brass coffee pot and a faded photograph of a young man standing beside a camel. Guests assumed it was a souvenir, and children were warned never to touch it. "My father found it in the sands to the south, the year the rains failed," Grandfather would say, before quickly changing the subject. This winter, however, Noura was sixteen, her Earth science teacher had just set a research project, and she had finally run out of patience with family mysteries.

"May I hold it, Jiddo?" she asked one Friday evening, and to everyone's surprise, he nodded. The stone was far heavier than it looked, as if it had been made of solid metal rather than rock. Its surface was covered in shallow dents, like thumbprints pressed into soft clay. "It's just a piece of an old volcano," said her thirteen-year-old brother Saad, barely looking up from his phone. Noura wasn't so sure, because she had seen a stone exactly like this in a textbook photograph, and the caption beneath it had made her heart beat faster.

She borrowed a magnet from the fridge and held it near the stone, and it jumped from her fingers with a loud click. Saad put his phone down. "Volcanic rock doesn't do that," Noura said quietly. "If I'm right, this thin black skin is a fusion crust, which forms when a meteoroid enters the atmosphere so fast that its outer layer melts." The dents, she explained, were carved by the burning air as the object fell, which was why scientists sometimes called them thumbprints.

Still, Noura knew that excitement was not the same as evidence. The next morning her teacher, Ms. Al-Harbi, listened carefully and then warned her not to jump to conclusions. "Most stones people bring to experts turn out to be industrial slag or magnetic iron ore," she said. "Only a proper laboratory could confirm it, so why don't you contact the geology department at the university in Riyadh?" Noura wrote a polite email with photographs attached, knowing it was a long shot, and then waited through three weeks of silence.

When the reply finally arrived, it came from a Dr. Reem Al-Qahtani, who wanted to examine the stone in person. Noura was thrilled, but Grandfather's face grew serious. "It belonged to my father," he said. "I won't have it smashed to pieces by strangers in white coats." Only after Dr. Reem promised on the phone that she would remove nothing bigger than a fingernail did he agree, and even then on one condition: he would be coming too.

The laboratory hummed with machines, and Saad, who had insisted on joining them, looked around as though he had walked onto a spaceship. A scanner revealed that the stone was about ninety-two percent iron and seven percent nickel, a combination rarely found in natural Earth rocks. Then Dr. Reem polished a tiny cut face and covered it with a weak acid. Slowly, a pattern of criss-crossing silver lines appeared, like woven palm leaves. "This forms only when metal cools incredibly slowly, perhaps a few degrees every million years, deep inside the core of a young asteroid," she said. "It simply cannot happen on Earth."

For a long moment, Grandfather said nothing at all. "So my father carried a piece of another world home on his camel," he murmured at last. Dr. Reem smiled and explained that the metal was probably around four and a half billion years old, older than any rock on our planet. "That makes it the oldest thing in our house," Saad said, "even older than Jiddo's jokes," and for once Grandfather laughed louder than anyone. Then Dr. Reem asked whether she could register the meteorite in the international database, where every meteorite is named after the place it was found.

That was the problem, because nobody knew exactly where it had been found. Back home, Grandfather disappeared into a back room and returned with a cracked leather notebook that had belonged to his father. Inside was a pencil sketch showing a dark dune, an old well and three acacia trees, with the words "Naqa Al-Sawda" written underneath. Noura spent two evenings comparing the sketch with satellite images until she spotted the same dark dune beside a dried-up well, exactly where the drawing had placed it. When she sent the coordinates to Dr. Reem, the reply came within an hour: there might be more fragments, and a spring expedition was being planned, which Noura was invited to join.

Noura's project won first prize at the regional science fair, but that wasn't the part she would remember most. The black stone returned to its shelf in the majlis, now with a small card beside it reading "Naqa Al-Sawda Meteorite, iron, found 1950s." These days Grandfather tells its full story to every guest, and he even lets the children hold it. Some nights, Noura climbs to the roof and gazes at the stars, wondering where the rest of that ancient asteroid is drifting now. Her great-grandfather had picked up a stone that had fallen from the sky, and decades later, she realised, it had fallen a second time, straight into her future.

pages.text: Sultan was a grey African parrot with bright red tail feathers, a sharp beak and, according to Omar's mother, absolutely no manners. He had belonged to Grandpa Saleh for twenty-two years, and when Grandpa moved in with the family in Riyadh, Sultan came too, cage, mirror and all. The bird knew about forty words, but hardly any of them were useful. He could imitate the microwave, the doorbell and Omar's mother shouting, "Omar, wake up, you'll be late!" so perfectly that Omar had once jumped out of bed at three o'clock in the morning.

One Sunday evening, Omar's father came home looking both proud and nervous. "Mr Al-Harbi, the new director of my company, has accepted our invitation to dinner on Thursday," he announced. "Everything has to be perfect, because this man could decide my future." Omar's mother slowly turned to look at the cage in the corner of the living room. "Then that bird is a recipe for disaster," she said, but Grandpa Saleh folded his arms and insisted that Sultan was a member of the family and would not be hidden away like a dirty plate.

To keep the peace, Omar came up with a plan. "Give me three days," he said confidently, "and I'll teach Sultan to say 'Welcome, honoured guest.' Mr Al-Harbi will be so impressed that he'll give Dad a promotion on the spot." His father didn't look convinced, but he was desperate enough to agree. That night, Omar watched a dozen online tutorials about bird training, which all recommended patience, repetition and plenty of sunflower seeds as rewards.

By Tuesday, Omar had repeated the phrase at least three hundred times, and Sultan had learned precisely nothing. Instead, the parrot had mastered the sound of Omar's phone notification and an extremely realistic cough. Omar's patience was wearing thin, and he began muttering under his breath, "Come on, you feathery potato, just say it!" His little sister Lama, who was supposedly doing her homework on the sofa, could not stop giggling. "If he learns anything," she warned him, "it won't be the polite part."

On Thursday evening the house was sparkling, the scent of incense filled the hallway, and a tray of Arabic coffee and dates was waiting in the majlis. Mr Al-Harbi turned out to be a tall, serious man with a neat grey beard and a voice so deep it seemed to make the windows tremble. Omar was on pins and needles as the guest walked past Sultan's cage. To everyone's relief, the parrot simply stared at him in complete silence, as if he were judging the man's choice of shoes.

Dinner went surprisingly well, and by the time Mr Al-Harbi reached for a second helping of kabsa, Omar's father had finally started to relax. Then, from the corner of the room, came a polite little cough that sounded exactly like Omar's. Every head turned towards the cage. "Come on, you feathery potato!" Sultan shrieked, staring straight at the guest. "Just say it!" Mr Al-Harbi's spoon froze halfway to his mouth, and Omar's father went as pale as the rice.

Before anyone could react, Sultan added the beep of the microwave and a perfect "Omar, wake up, you'll be late!" for good measure. Omar wished the floor would open up and swallow him whole. Grandpa Saleh cleared his throat to apologise, but suddenly Mr Al-Harbi burst into laughter so loud and so long that tears ran down his cheeks. "When I was a boy," he gasped, wiping his eyes, "my father had a parrot that shouted 'The food is burnt!' every single time my aunt came to visit, and she never forgave him."

After that, the atmosphere changed completely, as if someone had opened a window in a stuffy room. Mr Al-Harbi and Grandpa Saleh spent the rest of the evening swapping stories about clever birds, and the serious director even fed Sultan a sunflower seed through the bars of the cage. Omar's father, who had been sitting as stiffly as a statue, began to laugh along with them. Just before dessert, Mr Al-Harbi leaned towards Omar and whispered with a wink, "Promise me you'll never tell anyone at the office that I was called a potato."

It was nearly midnight when the guest finally stood at the front door, shaking hands and thanking the family for a wonderful evening. At that exact moment, Sultan spread his wings and cried out loud and clear, "Welcome, honoured guest!" The whole family collapsed into laughter, and Grandpa Saleh shook his head fondly. "His timing has always been terrible," he said, glancing at Omar, "a bit like yours." Omar sighed and announced that next time he would teach the bird to stay quiet, but Sultan simply tilted his head and replied, "Feathery potato."

stories.title: The Boy Who Listened to Trees

pages.text: Every summer, Yousef spent his mornings on his grandfather's farm outside Buraydah, where rows of date palms stood like patient soldiers beneath the blazing sky. This year, however, something was wrong. Three of the oldest palms, trees his grandfather had planted before Yousef's father was even born, had begun to lean, and their fronds were turning a sickly yellow. "The weevil," Grandfather Saleh said quietly, pressing his hand against the rough trunk. "By the time you can see the damage, it is usually too late."

That evening, Yousef couldn't get the dying trees out of his head. He read that the red palm weevil lays its eggs deep inside the trunk, where the larvae spend months eating the tree from the inside out, completely hidden from view. Farmers often discovered an infestation only when a tree finally collapsed. One sentence in an old research article, however, caught his eye: the larvae chewed so hard that, in theory, you could actually hear them. "If you can hear them," Yousef murmured, "you can catch them before it's too late."

His workshop was a corner of the family majlis that his mother had reluctantly given up, on condition that he kept it tidy. Over the next two weeks, he took apart an old phone, a cheap pair of headphones and a broken baby monitor that his cousin had been about to throw away. He connected a tiny microphone to a metal spike that could be pushed into a trunk, then wrote a simple program to filter out the wind and birdsong. His older sister Noura, who was studying engineering at university, raised an eyebrow when she saw the tangle of wires. "It looks like a spider got lost in a toolbox," she teased, but she stayed up late helping him fix the code anyway.

The first test was a complete disaster. Yousef pushed the spike into one of the sick palms, put on the headphones and heard absolutely nothing except his own heartbeat. He tried again in the afternoon, and once more the following morning, but the screen showed only flat, silent lines. Feeling foolish, he began to wonder whether he had been chasing an impossible idea all along. "Maybe the article was wrong," he admitted, kicking at the sand. Grandfather Saleh simply poured him a small cup of coffee and said, "A farmer who gives up after one season never tastes his own dates."

In the end, it was Noura who spotted the problem. "You're testing in the heat of the day," she pointed out, "when the farm is full of noise: the water pumps, the trucks on the road, the workers." She suggested they return after Isha prayer, by which time the farm would have fallen silent. So that night, under a sky crowded with stars, Yousef pressed the spike into the trunk once more and held his breath. At first there was only a soft hum, but then, faint but unmistakable, came a steady crunching sound, like someone slowly eating a biscuit inside a wall.

Yousef nearly dropped the phone. The crunching was loudest at one particular spot, and by moving the spike around, he could map exactly where the larvae were feeding. Over the following nights, he tested every palm on the farm, recording the results carefully in a notebook. Most trees were silent and healthy, but one young palm near the well, which looked perfectly green and strong, was crunching loudly. "Impossible," said his grandfather, frowning. "That tree is the healthiest one I have."

Grandfather Saleh was not a man who trusted gadgets, yet he trusted his grandson. He called an agricultural expert from the city, who drilled carefully into the young palm at the exact spot Yousef had marked. Inside, just as the device had predicted, dozens of fat, pale larvae were busily tunnelling through the wood. Because the infestation had been caught so early, the tree could be treated and saved. The expert turned the homemade device over in her hands and asked, "Have you ever thought about entering this in the national science competition?"

Two months later, Yousef stood nervously beside his poster in a vast hall in Riyadh, surrounded by robots, drones and inventions far shinier than his own. Some of the judges smiled politely at his tangle of wires, and he felt his confidence drain away. Then an elderly professor put on the headphones and listened to the recording from that night on the farm. His expression changed completely. "Do you realise," he said slowly, "that farmers across the region lose huge numbers of palms to this insect every year?"

Yousef didn't win first prize; he came third, and was offered support to develop a cheaper, stronger version of his device. Yet the moment he remembered most happened weeks later, back on the farm, beside the palm near the well. Its new fronds were bright and healthy, and a farmer from the next village had come to ask whether "the boy with the listening machine" could check his trees too. Grandfather Saleh rested a hand on Yousef's shoulder and smiled. "My father taught me to read the trees with my eyes," he said. "You have learned to listen to them."

pages.text: Faris had always assumed that his grandfather's old leather notebook was full of shopping lists, until the evening the old man placed it in his hands and asked him to read the last page aloud. In faded blue ink, it said: 'Ma'an, 1974. I owe Abu Yousef forty dinars and my life. I will return.' His grandfather explained quietly that he had never kept that promise, and that the thought had been weighing on him for fifty years. 'My eyes are tired and my memory is full of holes,' he admitted, 'but you, Faris, are sixteen and stubborn. Will you be my eyes?' Two weeks later, with his father's blessing, they were boarding a flight to Amman.

On the long road south, his grandfather finally told him the whole story. As a young man travelling to Jordan to look for work, he had taken a crowded bus that broke down in the middle of the desert, miles from anywhere. By the time he had walked to the nearest town, he had heatstroke, empty pockets and no idea where he was. A tea seller called Abu Yousef had found him collapsed near his shop, taken him home and looked after him for three days. 'When I left, he pressed forty dinars into my hand and refused to listen to my objections,' his grandfather said, staring out at the sand. 'I swore I would come back, but life got in the way, as it always does.'

Ma'an, however, was not the sleepy town his grandfather remembered. New buildings had sprung up everywhere, the roads had been widened, and the old market had apparently been knocked down years ago. Faris asked shopkeeper after shopkeeper about a tea seller named Abu Yousef, but most of them simply shrugged or laughed kindly. 'Abu Yousef?' one young man repeated. 'Half the men in this town are called that!' By sunset, Faris was beginning to feel that they were looking for a needle in a haystack.

That night in their small hotel, Faris refused to give up and went through the notebook page by page, searching for anything he might have missed. Hidden among notes about prices and bus times, he found a rough sketch: a shop with a striped awning, standing opposite a mosque with an unusually short minaret. Beside it, his grandfather had written, 'Water from the well with the green door.' It wasn't much to go on, but it was a great deal more than they had had that morning. Faris showed it to the hotel receptionist, who studied it for a long moment before her face lit up.

'My grandmother would know,' she said, and before Faris could protest, she had phoned her. The old lady remembered the short minaret immediately; it belonged to one of the oldest mosques in the town, which had been carefully restored rather than replaced. 'The well has been gone for decades,' she told them, 'but the family with the green door still lives on that street.' Early the next morning, Faris and his grandfather set off on foot, the old man leaning heavily on his grandson's arm. Neither of them said much, but Faris could feel his grandfather's hand trembling.

The mosque was exactly as the sketch had shown it, small and dignified among the modern buildings around it. Directly opposite, where the tea shop should have been, stood a bright little café with glass windows and a coffee machine that hissed like a snake. Faris's heart sank, and he was about to suggest they ask the neighbours instead when his grandfather suddenly stopped dead. Above the café's door, faded but unmistakable, hung a striped awning. 'He kept it,' the old man whispered. 'Somebody kept it.'

Inside, a man in his thirties was arranging cups behind the counter, and he greeted them warmly. When Faris explained, a little awkwardly, why they had come, the man's polite smile froze on his face. Without a word, he pointed to the wall, where a framed black-and-white photograph hung among newer pictures of the café. It showed an older man in a traditional headdress standing beside a thin, exhausted-looking young man who was holding a glass of tea. 'That is my grandfather, Abu Yousef,' the café owner said slowly. 'And for as long as I can remember, my family has wondered who that stranger was.'

Faris's grandfather sat down heavily, tears running freely down his lined face, and took an envelope from his pocket. Inside were four old ten-dinar notes, which he had kept for half a century so that he could return them exactly as they had been given. Yousef, the café owner, shook his head at once. 'My grandfather passed away twelve years ago, and he would never have accepted payment for kindness,' he insisted. 'But he used to say that a young man from Arabia would come back one day, and nobody believed him.' The two men embraced, and Faris, who had never seen his grandfather cry, found that his own eyes were stinging.

In the end, they reached a compromise that satisfied everyone. The four old notes were framed and hung beside the photograph, with a small card that read: 'A debt of honour, repaid in 2024.' Before they left, Yousef made them tea in the old way, in a dented brass pot that had once belonged to his grandfather. On the drive back to Amman, Faris's grandfather slept peacefully for the first time in days, the notebook resting on his chest. Faris watched the desert roll past and realised that some journeys are not measured in kilometres, but in the promises we keep.

pages.text: Faisal found the robot half-buried under broken air conditioners at the scrapyard on the edge of town. It was a solar-panel cleaner, long and flat like a metal tortoise, with a soft brush underneath and a cracked camera for an eye. The scrapyard owner laughed when Faisal asked the price, calling it 'a pile of junk that should have been recycled years ago.' Even so, Faisal handed over the money he had been saving since Ramadan and dragged his prize home in a wheelbarrow. His grandfather, sitting in the shade of the date palms, raised an eyebrow and said nothing, which in Faisal's experience was far worse than a lecture.

For two weeks, Faisal spent every spare hour in the small workshop beside the courtyard. His older sister Noura, who was studying computer science at university, agreed to help with the software on the condition that he stopped borrowing her laptop charger. Together they replaced the battery, cleaned out years of sand and rewired the damaged motor. On the fifteenth evening, the robot's camera flickered blue and its motors hummed into life. In a calm, slightly crackly voice, it announced, 'Row four hundred and twelve: incomplete. Resuming task.'

'Machines don't have duties,' Grandfather declared at dinner, tearing a piece of bread in half. 'They have batteries, and when the batteries run out, they stop.' Yet Faisal noticed that the old man kept glancing out of the window at the robot, which had rolled to the courtyard gate and was pressing patiently against it. Every time Faisal turned it around, it quietly turned itself back towards the east. 'Perhaps it's homesick,' Noura joked, but nobody laughed.

Late that night, Noura managed to open the robot's memory logs, and what she found made her sit up straight. Five years earlier, the robot had worked at a solar farm twenty kilometres east of town, which had been abandoned after a violent sandstorm damaged its control station. The robot had been halfway along Row 412 when its connection was suddenly cut. 'It's been waiting all this time to finish the job,' she whispered. She also discovered that, using radar rather than its camera, it had mapped every dune, rock and track between the farm and the town.

The next afternoon, Grandfather drove out to check on the family's camels, which were spending the winter at a camp not far from the old solar farm. He waved away Faisal's offer to come along, insisting that he had known that desert since before Faisal's father was born. By four o'clock, however, the sky had turned an ugly shade of orange, and the radio was warning of a severe sandstorm. When Faisal's father tried to call Grandfather, the phone simply rang and rang. Then the signal disappeared completely.

As the wind began to howl, the robot started beeping urgently in the workshop, its camera pointing east. 'Row 412,' it repeated. 'Route available.' Suddenly, the pieces fell into place in Faisal's mind. 'Dad, it doesn't need to see the road. It knows the way by radar, and Grandfather is somewhere near its old farm!' His father hesitated for only a moment before grabbing the car keys, and the three of them lifted the robot into the back seat of the truck.

Out in the storm, the headlights barely reached a few metres ahead, and the sand hissed against the windows like rain. Faisal held the robot steady on his lap while it called out directions in its calm, crackly voice: 'Bear left. Rock ahead. Continue straight for two hundred metres.' His father followed every instruction without a word, his knuckles white on the steering wheel. After what felt like hours, the dark shapes of solar panels loomed out of the dust. Beside them, tilted at an awkward angle with one wheel buried in a dune, was Grandfather's truck.

Grandfather was tired, dusty and unusually quiet, but completely unharmed. He climbed into the back seat, looked at the robot for a long time and finally rested his hand on its scratched metal shell. 'It brought you here?' he asked, and Faisal nodded. By the time they reached home, the storm had blown itself out, and the morning sky was a clean, washed blue. Before anyone had even had breakfast, Grandfather announced that they were driving back to the solar farm, because a promise was a promise.

They watched together as the robot rolled slowly to the end of Row 412, brushing five years of sand from the very last panel until it shone in the sunlight. 'Row 412: complete,' it said, and for once its voice sounded almost satisfied. 'He needs a proper name,' Grandfather said gruffly. 'We'll call him Wafi, because he keeps his word, which is more than I can say for some people.' These days, Wafi cleans the solar panels on the family's farmhouse roof, and every evening, Grandfather drinks his coffee beside him and tells him stories about the desert.

pages.text: Lama Al-Harbi had always believed that history belonged to kings, generals and the occasional poet whose verses were memorised by every schoolchild. So when her uncle, Dr. Khalid, invited her to spend the spring holiday with his archaeology team at Hegra, near AlUla, she agreed mainly because she was curious about the famous tombs. "Three weeks of brushing sand off rocks," her older brother Saud had teased before she left. "Try not to die of excitement." She had rolled her eyes, but secretly she was afraid he might be right.

On the first morning, her uncle took her to Qasr al-Farid, the enormous tomb carved from a single rock that stands alone in the desert. In the early light, its pale face glowed like honey. "The Nabataeans carved their tombs from the top downwards," he explained, pointing at the rough, unfinished base. "This one was never completed, and nobody knows why. Perhaps the owner died, or perhaps the money simply ran out." Lama tilted her head. "And the men who actually held the chisels? Do we know who they were?" Her uncle smiled a little sadly. "Occasionally a name survives, but usually the craftsmen have vanished without a trace."

For the next few days, Lama's job was to help record a low rock face that the team had nicknamed "the quiet corner", because nothing interesting had ever been found there. It was hot, slow work, and by Thursday she was beginning to suspect that Saud had a point. During a break, she sat in the shade of a fallen slab, eating dates and staring at the ground. That was when she noticed it: a thin, straight line in the stone beneath the slab, far too regular to have been made by wind. She leaned closer, her heart beating faster, and brushed away a little more sand.

Within minutes, the whole team had gathered around. Carefully, they cleared the area until a rough block appeared, covered in rows of scratched letters that looked as if they had been made by a nervous hand. "This isn't a formal inscription," her uncle murmured, his voice tight with excitement. "It looks like someone was practising." Just then, his phone buzzed, and his face changed. "A sandstorm is heading our way, and it'll be here within the hour," he announced. "We need to record everything before the wind buries it again."

They worked against the clock as the sky slowly turned the colour of rust. Photographs were taken from every angle, but the light was fading fast, and the shadows that made the letters readable were disappearing. Then, to make matters worse, the tablet they were using for measurements died. Without waiting to be asked, Lama pulled out her notebook and began copying the letters by hand, tracing each faint line with her finger before drawing it. Sand was stinging her face by the time her uncle shouted, "That's enough! Cover the stone and get to the car!"

For two long hours, they sat in the car while the storm roared outside, so thick that they couldn't even see the bonnet. Lama clutched her notebook, wondering whether she had copied anything correctly or whether she had just wasted everyone's time. "What if I got it all wrong?" she whispered. Her uncle shook his head firmly. "Every archaeologist makes mistakes, Lama, but the ones who give up never find anything at all. Whatever happens, you did the right thing."

The following morning, they discovered that the wind had torn the cover and half buried the block again, so the photographs alone were blurred and incomplete. However, when Dr. Nouf, the team's expert in ancient writing, compared them with Lama's drawings, the missing pieces fell into place. After an hour of silent concentration, she finally looked up and read aloud: "May Zaid, son of Hani'u, be remembered, who learned the chisel this year under his father. And may he not be lazy." For a moment, nobody spoke, and then the whole team burst out laughing. "Two thousand years later," Dr. Nouf said, wiping her eyes, "and fathers are still saying exactly the same thing."

That evening, Lama sat alone outside the camp, watching the stars appear over the silent tombs. She kept imagining Zaid: a boy perhaps her own age, his hands aching, his father watching over his shoulder as he scratched practice letters into a stone nobody was ever supposed to see. Had he helped to carve Qasr al-Farid? Had he grown up to become a master craftsman, or had he given it all up? She would never know, yet somehow he no longer felt like a stranger. It struck her that the great tombs might have been built for the powerful, but they had been made by people like Zaid.

Two weeks later, Dr. Khalid's official report described the discovery as "Zaid's Stone", and beneath it, in small but unmistakable print, was the line: "First identified and recorded by Lama Al-Harbi." She took a photo of the page and sent it to Saud with a single message: "Died of excitement. Highly recommended." His reply came almost immediately: a row of astonished faces, followed by "Okay, I take it back." Lama smiled and opened her notebook to a fresh page. History, she wrote, does not belong only to kings; it belongs to anyone patient enough to look beneath the sand.

Nice. How will you deal with people who say they're too busy?
I'll say: the question isn't whether we have time, but how we choose to use it.
Brilliant. And finish with something that unites everyone.
Surely we can all agree that giving back to our community is something to be proud of.

grammar.title: Negative inversion for emphasis
grammar.ar: عندما نبدأ الجملة بتعبير منفي أو مُقيِّد مثل 'Not only' أو 'Never' أو 'Rarely'، نقلب ترتيب الفاعل والفعل المساعد كما في السؤال. مثلاً: 'Not only does it help...' وليس 'Not only it helps...'. يُستخدم هذا الأسلوب في الخطابات والكتابة الرسمية لإضافة قوة وتأثير. إذا لم يكن هناك فعل مساعد، نضيف do/does/did.
examples: Not only does volunteering help others, but it also helps you grow.
Never have I felt so proud as when I volunteered at the festival.
Rarely do young people get such a chance to represent their city.

words.ex: My opponent made some interesting points, but I disagree.
Each team has two minutes for its rebuttal.
Many schools now use blended learning to combine classroom and online lessons.

words.ar: لا يمكن الاستغناء عنه أو تعويضه
words.ex: Face-to-face interaction with teachers is irreplaceable.
The weight of evidence suggests that students need social contact.
School helps children develop social skills they can't learn online.

dialogue.t: To open, I'd like to argue that online learning will never fully replace traditional schools, because school is about far more than lessons.
I disagree. Online learning is flexible, cheaper and available anywhere. Traditional schools are becoming outdated.
My opponent claims that online learning is more flexible, but flexibility means little if students lose motivation without a teacher present.
Many students actually prefer studying at their own pace at home.
Some do, admittedly. Let me return to my earlier point about social skills: teamwork and friendship simply can't be built through a screen.
Surely blended learning solves that problem, though?
Exactly, and that supports my case, because blended learning still needs physical schools.
To sum up, the weight of evidence clearly shows that technology will support schools, not replace them.

grammar.title: Reporting verbs for summarising an opponent's argument
grammar.ar: في المناظرة نحتاج إلى نقل رأي الخصم بدقة قبل الرد عليه، ونستخدم أفعالاً مثل claim (يدّعي)، argue (يجادل)، suggest (يقترح)، insist (يُصرّ)، maintain (يؤكد باستمرار). يدل الفعل claim على أننا نشكّ في صحة الكلام، بينما argue أكثر حياداً. نستخدم المضارع البسيط عادةً عند نقل رأي الخصم في المناظرة، ويتبع الفعلَ جملةٌ تبدأ بـ that.
examples: My opponent claims that online learning is cheaper, but the costs of devices are often ignored.
The other side argues that schools are outdated; however, they still provide vital social contact.
My opponent insists that students prefer studying alone, yet surveys show the opposite.

words.ar: لديه القدرة على / من المحتمل أن
words.ex: AI tools have the potential to make learning more personalised for every student.
Over-reliance on chatbots could weaken students' ability to think for themselves.
Teachers are worried that AI makes plagiarism much harder to detect.
Many banks have already automated simple customer service tasks.
Critical thinking is essential if you want to judge whether an AI answer is accurate.
Economists disagree about how much job displacement AI will actually cause.

dialogue.t: Have you noticed how many people in our class use AI for homework now?
Definitely. It's increasingly common for students to ask a chatbot before they even open the textbook.
Honestly, I think AI has the potential to be an amazing personal tutor, especially for difficult subjects like physics.
Maybe, but there's a real risk that we stop thinking for ourselves and just copy whatever it says.
That's fair. So whether this is beneficial depends largely on how we use it, right?
Exactly. If you use it to check your understanding, great. If you use it to avoid learning, that's a problem.
And what about future jobs? My uncle says AI will replace half the people in his office.
Some jobs will disappear, but new ones will appear too. The key is learning skills that machines can't easily copy, like creativity and empathy.

grammar.title: Whether-clauses as subjects
grammar.ar: نستخدم جملة تبدأ بـ whether كفاعل في الجملة عندما نتحدث عن أمر غير محسوم يعتمد على شروط معينة. يأتي بعدها فعل مفرد مثل depends أو remains. هذا الأسلوب يجعل رأيك متوازناً وأكثر رسمية، وهو مفيد جداً في اختبارات المحادثة مثل IELTS.
examples: Whether AI improves education depends largely on how teachers integrate it.
Whether these tools are safe for children remains a matter of debate.
Whether students benefit or not depends on their motivation to learn.

words.ex: Autonomous vehicles could make traffic accidents far less common.
NEOM aims to run entirely on renewable energy from the sun and wind.
A smart city needs reliable digital infrastructure to function.
In 2050, your daily commute might take just five minutes.
Planners want to design cities that are sustainable for future generations.
Petrol cars will probably be phased out in many cities by 2040.

dialogue.t: What do you think daily life in NEOM will be like in 2050?
By 2050, we'll probably have driverless pods instead of cars. No traffic jams at all!
That sounds amazing. It's highly likely that petrol cars will have been phased out completely by then.
I agree. And I wouldn't be surprised if every building generated its own solar power.
What about daily routines? Do you think people will still go to offices?
There's every chance that most people will work from home or from shared hubs near where they live.
I hope so. Commuting less would give families much more time together.
True, although I suspect some people will miss the social side of going to work.

grammar.title: Future perfect passive
grammar.ar: نستخدم المستقبل التام المبني للمجهول (will have been + التصريف الثالث) للحديث عن شيء سيكون قد اكتمل قبل وقت محدد في المستقبل، عندما لا يهمنا من قام بالفعل. غالباً نستخدم معه تعبيرات زمنية مثل by 2050 أو by then. ويمكن إضافة probably أو likely لتقليل درجة اليقين.
examples: By 2050, most traditional power stations will have been replaced by solar farms.
It's highly likely that the new railway will have been completed by 2035.
By the time we graduate, many old jobs will have been automated.

words.ex: Gene editing could one day eliminate certain inherited diseases.
Sickle cell anaemia is a hereditary disease that affects many families in the region.
Using genetics for enhancement, such as increasing intelligence, is highly controversial.
Many doctors have moral reservations about changing human embryos.
Allowing this experiment could set a precedent for riskier ones.
Scientists still don't fully understand the unintended consequences of editing genes.

dialogue.t: Did you read about scientists using gene editing to cure blood diseases?
Yes, and I think it's incredible if it stops children from suffering.
I agree, but where do we draw the line between treating illness and creating 'perfect' babies?
That's the difficult part. It raises serious ethical questions about who decides what 'normal' is.
Exactly. On moral grounds, I'd be reluctant to allow parents to choose things like height or intelligence.
Me too. And if only rich families could afford it, it could set a dangerous precedent.
So you'd support it for medical use only?
Yes, with strict regulation and plenty of research first, because we can't predict every long-term effect.

grammar.title: Expressing reservations with would + adjective
grammar.ar: نستخدم تراكيب مثل I'd be reluctant to و I'd be hesitant to و I'd be wary of للتعبير عن تحفظنا بأسلوب مهذب وغير حاد. يأتي بعد reluctant و hesitant فعل في المصدر مع to، بينما يأتي بعد wary of فعل بصيغة ing. هذا الأسلوب أكثر لباقة من قول I disagree مباشرة.
examples: On moral grounds, I'd be reluctant to support enhancement for non-medical reasons.
I'd be hesitant to approve the treatment without more evidence.
Many scientists would be wary of editing genes that are passed on to future generations.

words.ex: A photovoltaic cell turns sunlight directly into electricity.
An inverter converts direct current into alternating current.
Large solar farms can generate enough power for thousands of homes.
The electricity is then fed into the national grid.
Switching to solar power significantly reduces carbon emissions.
Sunshine is abundant in Saudi Arabia for most of the year.

dialogue.t: Can you explain how solar panels actually produce electricity? I've never really understood it.
Sure. The process begins when sunlight hits the photovoltaic cells in the panel.
And what happens inside the cells?
The light knocks electrons loose in the silicon, which creates a direct current. This is then converted into alternating current by an inverter.
So that's the kind of electricity we use at home?
Exactly. As a result of this, it can be sent to the national grid and used in houses, schools and factories.
Why is it so important for Saudi Arabia specifically?
What makes this particularly significant is that we have abundant sunshine, so solar power can help meet the Vision 2030 renewable energy targets.

grammar.title: Present simple passive for processes
grammar.ar: عند شرح عملية علمية أو صناعية نستخدم المضارع البسيط المبني للمجهول (is/are + التصريف الثالث) لأن التركيز يكون على العملية نفسها وليس على من يقوم بها. ونربط المراحل بكلمات مثل first و then و after that و finally. هذا يجعل الشرح واضحاً ومنظماً.
examples: Sunlight is absorbed by the silicon layer of the panel.
The direct current is then converted into alternating current.
Finally, the electricity is distributed to homes through the grid.

words.ex: Some apps collect personal data such as your location and contacts.
Companies should not use your information without your consent.
The data breach exposed millions of users' passwords.
Your data may be sold to third parties for advertising.
Tech companies must be held accountable when they misuse data.
It's a good idea to check your privacy settings every few months.

dialogue.t: Did you know that some free games track your location even when you're not playing?
Seriously? I think many users are unaware that they've agreed to that in the terms and conditions.
Nobody reads them! They're far too long. Should companies be held accountable for hiding things in small print?
Absolutely. It's essential that young people's data be protected by clear laws.
Remember that big data breach last year? Had people known how much information the app was storing, they might have deleted it.
True. That's why I always check app permissions before installing anything now.
What else can teenagers do to stay safe?
Use strong passwords, turn on two-factor authentication and think twice before sharing photos that show where you live.

grammar.title: The subjunctive after 'essential that'
grammar.ar: بعد عبارات مثل It's essential that و It's vital that و I recommend that نستخدم الفعل في صيغته المجردة (بدون s وبدون to) مهما كان الفاعل، وهذا يُسمى صيغة الطلب أو الـ subjunctive. ومع المبني للمجهول نستخدم be بدلاً من is أو are. هذا الأسلوب رسمي ويُستخدم للتعبير عن ضرورة أو مطالبة قوية.
examples: It's essential that children's personal data be protected.
Experts recommend that every user check their privacy settings regularly.
It's vital that each company explain clearly how it uses our information.

words.ex: We built a simple prototype to test whether the idea would work.
The judges asked whether the design was financially feasible.
The main drawback of the device is its high cost.
Shaded walkways could help alleviate the effects of summer heat.
Solar-powered cooling is becoming more cost-effective every year.
If the pilot succeeds, the company plans to scale up across the country.

dialogue.t: So, tell me about your invention. What problem does it solve?
If I could design anything, it would be a solar-powered smart umbrella that cools the air around you in summer.
Interesting. And how would that change people's lives?
Were this to become reality, people could walk outside comfortably even when it's forty-five degrees.
But is it really feasible? How would it stay cool without a big battery?
Small solar panels on top would power a mini fan and mist system. Supposing it worked, people would no longer need to drive very short distances just to avoid the heat.
That's clever. Are there any weaknesses you've considered?
The main drawback might be the price at first, but if we scaled up production, it would become much more affordable.

grammar.title: Inverted and alternative conditionals
grammar.ar: في الأسلوب الرسمي يمكن حذف if وقلب ترتيب الجملة، فنقول Were this to happen بدلاً من If this happened، و Had I known بدلاً من If I had known. كما يمكن استخدام Supposing أو Provided that بدلاً من if للحديث عن مواقف افتراضية. هذه التراكيب تجعل حديثك أكثر تقدماً وإقناعاً عند عرض الأفكار.
examples: Were this device to become affordable, every family could own one.
Supposing the government funded it, the project could start next year.
Should the prototype fail, we would redesign the cooling system.

words.ex: Diriyah is a heritage site that tells the story of the first Saudi state.
It's essential that we preserve ancient sites like Hegra for future generations.
Before I begin, let me give you a brief outline of my talk.
The historical significance of AlUla goes back thousands of years.
The restoration of At-Turaif has attracted visitors from all over the world.
Heritage sites help young people feel connected to their cultural identity.

dialogue.t: Okay, whenever you're ready, you can start your presentation.
Thank you. Good morning, everyone. Today I'm going to talk about why heritage sites such as AlUla and Diriyah matter so much.
I've divided my talk into three main parts.
First, I'll look at their historical significance, then move on to their role in tourism and the economy.
Finally, I'll consider how we can preserve them for future generations.
That's a very clear opening. Why did you decide to mention the outline so early?
Because I think the audience follows more easily when they know where the talk is going.
Exactly. A clear outline is like a map for your listeners.

grammar.title: Future forms for announcing a plan
grammar.ar: عند افتتاح العرض نستخدم going to للحديث عن خطة قررناها مسبقًا (Today I'm going to talk about...)، ونستخدم will المختصرة 'll لعرض خطوات الحديث بالترتيب (First, I'll look at...). ونستخدم المضارع التام I've divided لأن تقسيم العرض تمّ قبل لحظة الكلام ونتيجته حاضرة الآن. انتبه: لا نقول I will to talk، بل نضع الفعل بعد will مباشرة دون to.
examples: Today I'm going to talk about the importance of protecting historic buildings.
First, I'll look at the history of Diriyah, then move on to its restoration.
I've divided my presentation into three short sections.

words.ex: Participation in sports among Saudi girls has increased noticeably in recent years.
Spending hours on phones can lead to a sedentary lifestyle.
The school launched a new initiative to encourage students to join sports teams.
Hot weather is often seen as a barrier to outdoor exercise.
Many neighbourhoods now have better sports facilities than they did ten years ago.
Hosting major tournaments can boost young people's interest in sport.

dialogue.t: So, those are the main reasons why many teenagers aren't active enough. This brings me to my next point: what's changing.
Moving on to new initiatives, the number of sports academies and women's leagues has grown significantly.
Sorry to interrupt, but could you give an example?
Of course. Many schools now run after-school football and basketball programmes for both boys and girls.
Having looked at these initiatives, I'd now like to discuss the barriers that still exist.
Let's now turn our attention to the climate, since the summer heat makes outdoor sport difficult.
Your transitions were really smooth. I always knew exactly where you were in the talk.
Thanks! I practised linking each section so it didn't sound like a list.

grammar.title: Perfect participle clauses: Having + past participle
grammar.ar: نستخدم تركيب Having + التصريف الثالث للفعل لنوضّح أن فعلًا قد انتهى قبل فعل آخر، وهو أسلوب رسمي ممتاز للانتقال بين أجزاء العرض. مثلًا: Having looked at the causes تعني: بعد أن تناولنا الأسباب. يجب أن يكون الفاعل في الجملتين واحدًا (I)، فلا نقول: Having looked at the causes, the solutions are...
examples: Having looked at the benefits of sport, I'd now like to examine the challenges.
Having discussed the role of schools, let's turn to the role of parents.
Having analysed the survey results, we can draw some clear conclusions.

words.ex: There was a sharp rise in online shopping between 2019 and 2021.
Visitor numbers peaked during the winter season.
Hotel prices tend to fluctuate depending on the time of year.
The graph shows a steady increase in domestic tourism.
The growth can be attributed to the introduction of tourist e-visas.

words.ar: يستقر / يتوقف عن الارتفاع أو الانخفاض
words.ex: After years of rapid growth, the figures began to level off.

dialogue.t: Could you describe what this graph shows about e-commerce in Saudi Arabia?
Sure. There was a sharp rise in online sales between 2019 and 2021.
The figure peaked at around 70% of consumers shopping online in 2022, and then it levelled off slightly.
What do you think caused such rapid growth?
This trend can largely be attributed to the pandemic, when people had to stay at home and order everything online.
It's worth noting that faster delivery apps and digital payment methods also played a big role.
Good. Do you think the trend will continue?
Probably, but I'd expect a more gradual increase rather than another dramatic jump.

grammar.title: Describing trends: verb + adverb vs. adjective + noun
grammar.ar: يمكن وصف التغيّر في البيانات بطريقتين: فعل + ظرف (Sales rose sharply) أو صفة + اسم (There was a sharp rise in sales). لاحظ أن الظرف يصف الفعل وغالبًا ينتهي بـ ly، بينما الصفة تأتي قبل الاسم. التنويع بين الأسلوبين يجعل وصفك للرسم البياني أكثر احترافية ويرفع درجتك في اختبار IELTS.
examples: The number of tourists increased dramatically after 2019.
There was a dramatic increase in the number of tourists after 2019.
Online spending fell slightly in 2023 before recovering steadily.

words.ex: Could you clarify what you mean by sustainable tourism?
Sorry, could you rephrase the question? I didn't quite catch it.

words.w: off the top of my head
words.ar: من دون تحضير / على حدّ ما أتذكر الآن
words.ex: Off the top of my head, I'd say about half the students agreed.
That's a valid point, and it's something I hadn't fully considered.
Would you like me to elaborate on the economic benefits?
My argument is based on the assumption that visitor numbers will keep growing.

dialogue.t: Thanks for your talk. You mentioned that tourism helps local communities, but doesn't it also damage the environment?
That's an interesting question. If I understand you correctly, you're asking whether the benefits outweigh the environmental costs?
Yes, exactly.
I think it depends on how tourism is managed. In AlUla, for example, visitor numbers are controlled to protect the sites.
And how much money does tourism actually bring to local families?
I'm not entirely sure, but I'd imagine it's significant, since many locals now work as guides or run small businesses.
What about the effect on traditional ways of life?
That's a valid point. I'll come back to that point in a moment, because it links to my final slide.

grammar.title: Indirect (embedded) questions
grammar.ar: عندما نعيد صياغة سؤال شخص آخر نستخدم السؤال غير المباشر، وفيه يكون ترتيب الكلمات مثل الجملة الخبرية (الفاعل ثم الفعل) وليس مثل السؤال. فنقول: you're asking what the main problem is وليس what is the main problem. وإذا كان السؤال الأصلي يُجاب بنعم أو لا نستخدم whether أو if. هذا خطأ شائع لدى متحدثي العربية فانتبه له.
examples: If I understand you correctly, you're asking why the numbers dropped in 2020.
You're asking whether tourism has a negative impact on local culture.
Could you tell me what exactly you mean by long-term benefits?

words.ex: Engineering graduates usually have excellent job prospects.
She chose to study art because it's her real passion.
Hearing a parent's perspective made me rethink my choice.
There's often a trade-off between a high salary and doing what you love.
Internships can greatly improve a graduate's employability.
A fulfilling career keeps you motivated for years.

dialogue.t: In my view, students should follow their passion, because they'll work harder at something they enjoy.
Building on what you said, motivation could actually lead to better job prospects in the long run.
Exactly. People who love their field tend to become experts.
However, I'd like to add a slightly different perspective. Some fields have very few jobs, so passion alone might not be enough.
That's fair. To what extent do you think universities should guide students towards high-demand majors?
To some extent, yes. That ties in with Vision 2030, which is creating demand in areas like tourism, tech and renewable energy.
So perhaps the ideal is finding a passion that also matches the job market.
Arguably, yes. It's a trade-off, but the two don't have to be opposites.

grammar.title: Hedging: softening your opinions
grammar.ar: في النقاش الأكاديمي نتجنب العبارات القاطعة جدًا، ونستخدم أدوات التلطيف (hedging) مثل might وcould وtend to وarguably وto some extent. هذا يجعل رأيك يبدو مدروسًا ومهذبًا، ويفتح المجال للنقاش بدلًا من الجدال. قارن: Passion is more important (قاطع) مع Passion is arguably more important (أكثر أكاديمية).
examples: Students who follow their passion tend to perform better at university.
Choosing a major only for money could arguably lead to burnout.
To some extent, job prospects should influence our decisions.

words.ex: Let me quickly recap the three main causes of food waste.
A strong call to action tells the audience exactly what they can do.
Social media campaigns can raise awareness of mental health issues.
She ended her talk with a compelling personal story.
Each of us needs to take responsibility for the waste we produce.
Even small changes in our daily habits can make a difference.

dialogue.t: To recap the main points, we waste huge amounts of food at gatherings, it harms the environment, and simple solutions already exist.
What this clearly shows is that food waste isn't just a big-company problem; it starts in our own homes.
I'd like to leave you with one thought: if every family cooked just a little less for each gathering, imagine the difference we could make.
So this week, try sharing leftovers with neighbours or donating them to a food bank.
Thank you for listening. Are there any questions?
Yes. That was a very compelling ending. Why did you choose food waste as your topic?
Because I noticed how much food is left after big family dinners, and I wanted to raise awareness among people my age.
Well, your call to action was clear and practical. Great job.

grammar.title: Cleft sentences for emphasis: What ... is ...
grammar.ar: نستخدم الجمل المشطورة (cleft sentences) لتسليط الضوء على فكرة مهمة، خصوصًا في خاتمة العرض. التركيب هو: What + فاعل + فعل + is/was + الفكرة المؤكَّدة. فبدلًا من This shows that we must act نقول What this shows is that we must act، فتصبح الجملة أقوى وتجذب انتباه الجمهور إلى النقطة الأساسية.
examples: What this clearly shows is that young people can lead real change.
What we really need is more awareness, not more rules.
What surprised me most was how easy the solutions are.

words.ex: My hometown has become a bustling city with new malls and cafés everywhere.
People in my neighbourhood are quite laid-back, so life feels less stressful there.
I took up photography last year after my uncle lent me his old camera.
My chemistry course is really demanding, but I find it rewarding.
After a long day at school, I usually unwind by playing football with my friends.
I've always been keen on languages, especially English and French.

dialogue.t: Let's talk about your hometown. Do you like living there?
To be honest, I'd say I really love it because it's grown so much in recent years. It's a bustling place now, but the people are still friendly and laid-back.
Do you prefer studying in the morning or in the evening?

It depends, really. On the one hand, my mind is fresher in the morning, but on the other, I'm more relaxed at night when the house is quiet. So I usually do revision in the morning and reading in the evening.
What do you like doing in your free time?
What I particularly enjoy is cycling along the corniche with my cousins. It helps me unwind after a demanding week at school.
Have your hobbies changed since you were a child?
Yes, quite a lot. I used to spend hours playing video games, but these days I'm much more keen on outdoor activities. I think I've realised how important it is to stay active.

grammar.title: Used to for past habits and states
grammar.ar: نستخدم used to + الفعل في صيغته الأساسية للحديث عن عادات أو حالات كانت تحدث في الماضي ولم تعد تحدث الآن، وهي تشبه في العربية «كنتُ أفعل». في النفي والسؤال نستخدم did ونحذف حرف d فنقول didn't use to و Did you use to. يمكن ربطها بعبارة but these days أو nowadays لتوضيح التغيير بين الماضي والحاضر، مما يجعل إجابتك أطول وأكثر تطوراً.
examples: I used to live in a small village, but these days I live in Riyadh.
I didn't use to enjoy reading, but now I read a novel every month.
Did you use to play any sports when you were younger?

words.ex: My older sister has always been a role model for me because she works so hard.

words.ar: مرشد أو موجّه يقدم النصح والخبرة
words.ex: My science teacher acted as a mentor and helped me choose my future career.

words.ar: يسعى إلى تحقيق هدف أو متابعة مجال
words.ex: She encouraged me to pursue my dream of becoming an engineer.
Winning that competition was a real turning point in my life.
He taught me to persevere even when things didn't go according to plan.
Her story inspired me to start volunteering at the local hospital.

dialogue.t: Now, I'd like you to describe a person who has influenced your goals. You have one minute to prepare, then speak for up to two minutes.
I'd like to talk about my maths teacher in Grade 9, Mr Khalid. He wasn't just a teacher; he was more like a mentor to me.
What struck me most was his patience. Whenever I struggled with a problem, he never gave me the answer directly. Instead, he asked questions until I worked it out myself.
One day he showed our class a video about engineers designing new cities in Saudi Arabia. It was at that point that I realised I wanted to pursue engineering myself.
He also taught me to persevere. I failed my first big test that year, but he told me that mistakes are just part of learning.
Looking back, I think the reason it mattered was that he believed in me before I believed in myself. That was a real turning point.
Thank you. Do you still keep in touch with him?
Yes, occasionally. I sent him a message when I got my exam results, and he was really proud.

grammar.title: Cleft sentences for emphasis
grammar.ar: الجمل المشقوقة (Cleft sentences) هي طريقة لإبراز معلومة معينة وجعلها محور الاهتمام. نستخدم تركيب It was ... that ... لتأكيد زمن أو شخص أو سبب، وتركيب What ... was ... لتأكيد فكرة أو شعور. هذه التراكيب تُظهر للممتحن مدى تنوع قواعدك وتجعل حديثك أكثر تأثيراً ووضوحاً.
examples: It was at that point that I realised I wanted to become a doctor.
What struck me most was how calm she stayed under pressure.
It was my grandfather who first encouraged me to read.

words.ar: بيئة أو مكان يحدث فيه شيء
words.ex: The first photo shows students learning in a formal classroom setting.
I prefer hands-on activities like science experiments to just reading a textbook.
The boy seems completely engrossed in his project.
She looks a bit frustrated, perhaps because the task is too difficult.
Learning outdoors can be fun, but there are more distractions.
The students in the second picture are collaborating on a group task.

dialogue.t: Here are your two photographs. They show people learning in different situations. Compare the photographs and say how the people might be feeling.
Both pictures show young people learning, whereas the settings are completely different. The first one is a traditional classroom, while the second is outdoors, maybe on a school trip.
The people in the first photo seem to be listening to a lecture. One girl is taking notes, but the boy next to her looks a little bored.
In the second photo, the students are doing something hands-on. They might well be feeling more motivated because they're collaborating and moving around.
Judging by their expressions, they're really engrossed in the activity. However, there could be more distractions outside, like noise or the heat.
Thank you. Which of these ways of learning would you prefer?
Personally, I'd choose the outdoor one, because I remember things better when I actually experience them.

grammar.title: Modal verbs for speculation
grammar.ar: عندما لا نكون متأكدين مما نراه في الصورة، نستخدم أفعال الاحتمال (modal verbs) للتخمين. نستخدم must be عندما نكون شبه متأكدين، و might/may/could be عندما يكون الأمر محتملاً، و can't be عندما نكون متأكدين أن الشيء غير صحيح. إضافة كلمة well بعد might أو may تعني أن الاحتمال قوي، مثل: They might well be tired.
examples: They might well be feeling nervous because it looks like an exam.
She must be enjoying herself; she's smiling the whole time.
He can't be very interested, judging by the way he's looking at his phone.

words.ex: I think the school should prioritise students' health over appearance.
Building a swimming pool isn't really feasible because it's too expensive.

words.ar: فعّال من حيث التكلفة، يحقق نتيجة جيدة بتكلفة قليلة
words.ex: Planting trees is a cost-effective way to make the playground cooler.
The main drawback of a new cafeteria is the time it would take to build.
You have a point, but I still think the library needs more attention.
After discussing all the options, we finally reached an agreement.

dialogue.t: Shall we start with the idea of adding more green spaces? I think it would make the school feel much more welcoming.
I agree. Plants would also give some shade in summer. What's your take on renovating the library?
Well, it would encourage reading, but it might not benefit everyone. Some students hardly ever use it.
That's a good point, but don't you think a modern library with computers and quiet study rooms would attract more students?
Maybe, but the drawback is the cost. Green spaces seem more cost-effective and feasible in the short term.
You have a point. And everyone would benefit from them, not just people who like reading.
So, are we agreed that creating more green spaces would be the most effective?
Yes, I think we've reached an agreement. Green spaces it is.

grammar.title: Negative questions to persuade
grammar.ar: نستخدم الأسئلة المنفية مثل Don't you think ...? و Wouldn't it be better ...? لنعرض رأينا بطريقة مهذبة ونحاول إقناع الطرف الآخر دون أن نبدو عدوانيين. هذه الأسئلة لا تطلب معلومة فعلاً، بل تتوقع أن يوافق المستمع. وهي مفيدة جداً في الجزء الثالث من اختبار B2 First لأنها تُظهر التفاعل والتعاون مع الشريك.
examples: Don't you think a bigger cafeteria would solve the problem?
Wouldn't it be better to ask the students what they want first?
Isn't it true that sports facilities help students stay healthy?

words.ex: In the past, most Saudis lived with their extended family in one large house.
Nowadays, many young couples prefer to live as a nuclear family in their own flat.
The number of women in the Saudi workforce has increased significantly.
Saudi society has gone through a remarkable transformation in the last decade.
Even as society modernises, many families work hard to uphold traditions.
Learning English can greatly improve your career prospects.

dialogue.t: How have family roles changed in Saudi Arabia in recent years?
Generally speaking, they've become more flexible. In the past, fathers were usually the only earners, but now many mothers are part of the workforce too.
Why do you think that is?
There are several reasons for this. Firstly, there are far more job opportunities for women. Secondly, the cost of living has risen, so many families need two incomes.
Do you think young people today have different attitudes towards education?
Definitely. Compared with previous generations, young people nowadays are much more focused on their career prospects, and many want to study abroad.
What effect might these changes have on society?
In the long run, this could lead to a more competitive economy. However, I hope families will still uphold traditions, like gathering with the extended family every weekend.

grammar.title: Comparatives with modifiers
grammar.ar: عند المقارنة بين الماضي والحاضر، يمكننا تقوية الصفة المقارنة أو إضعافها باستخدام كلمات معدِّلة. نستخدم far / much / considerably للدلالة على فرق كبير، و slightly / a bit للدلالة على فرق صغير. كما يمكن استخدام عبارة Compared with ... في بداية الجملة. هذا الأسلوب يجعل إجاباتك أكثر دقة ويرفع درجتك في القواعد والمفردات.
examples: Compared with previous generations, young people nowadays are far more independent.
Education is considerably more important for getting a job than it used to be.
Families today are slightly smaller than they were thirty years ago.

words.ex: Try to give coherent answers by linking your ideas with words like 'however' and 'as a result'.
There was some hesitation in your answer, but overall your fluency was good.
If you forget a word, just paraphrase it instead of stopping.
Using idioms and less common words shows a wide range of vocabulary.

words.ar: التنغيم، أي ارتفاع الصوت وانخفاضه أثناء الكلام
words.ex: Good intonation makes you sound more natural and engaging.
The examiner wants you to elaborate rather than give one-word answers.

dialogue.t: Let's move on. Do you think teenagers should be allowed to choose their own subjects at school?
I've never really thought about that, but I suppose it would make students more motivated. Not only would they enjoy school more, but they would also perform better.
Will technology replace teachers in the future?
It's hard to say, although I suppose some tasks, like marking tests, could be done by computers. But students still need a human to inspire them.
Imagine a friend wanted to drop out of school to start a business. What would you say?
If I were in that situation, I would advise him to finish school first. He could still develop his business idea in his free time.
That's the end of the test. Your answers were coherent and you elaborated well. Your range of vocabulary was strong, but watch your intonation; it was a bit flat sometimes.
Thank you. I'll try to vary my voice more and reduce my hesitation next time.

grammar.title: Inversion with 'Not only ... but also'
grammar.ar: يمكن استخدام Not only ... but also بطريقتين: الطريقة العادية مثل He is not only clever but also kind، أو بطريقة القلب (inversion) عند وضع Not only في بداية الجملة، وهنا يجب تقديم الفعل المساعد على الفاعل كما في السؤال. مثلاً: Not only does she speak English, but she also speaks French. هذا التركيب المتقدم يُظهر للممتحن مستوى عالياً في القواعد ويرفع درجتك.
examples: Not only does exercise keep you fit, but it also improves your mood.
Not only would a new library help students, but it would also benefit the community.
Not only did she pass the exam, but she also got the highest score in her class.
